title: Detergent Used Instead of Salt in Bihar Mid-Day Meal, Over 25 Students Fall Ill
excerpt: Children at a government school in Nalanda district complained of vomiting and dizziness after consuming the contaminated meal, the latest in a string of food safety failures in Bihar's school nutrition programme.
body:
• More than 25 children fell ill at Parasi Middle School in the Noorsarai area of Nalanda district, Bihar, after detergent powder was mistakenly used instead of salt in the mid-day meal.
  • Students complained of vomiting, dizziness, and stomach pain shortly after consuming the food on August 19.
  • Bihar has seen a pattern of mid-day meal contamination incidents, including 60 children falling ill in Nalanda in May 2026 — prompting an NHRC intervention.
  • India's mid-day meal scheme feeds approximately 120 million schoolchildren daily, making food safety lapses a systemic concern.

More than two dozen schoolchildren fell ill on Tuesday after consuming the mid-day meal at Parasi Middle School in the Noorsarai police station area of Nalanda district, Bihar. Preliminary reports indicate that detergent powder was mistakenly used in place of salt during food preparation, leading to widespread panic among parents and school staff.

What Happened

Students began complaining of vomiting, dizziness, and abdominal pain shortly after eating the school-provided lunch. The affected children were rushed to nearby health facilities for treatment. While the exact number of students taken ill varies across reports — some accounts cite 25, others put the figure closer to 36 — the cause appears consistent: a cook inadvertently mixed detergent powder into the food, mistaking it for salt.

https://x.com/NewsArenaIndia/status/2089734466155725278

The incident bears a disturbing resemblance to a September 2022 case at Chilimpur Primary School in West Bengal's North Dinajpur district, where a cook made the identical error. In that incident, 12 students fell ill after consuming khichuri laced with detergent. The cook was removed from duty, and all children recovered.

A Pattern in Bihar

Tuesday's incident is the latest in a troubling series of food safety failures in Bihar's schools. In May 2026, approximately 60 schoolchildren in Nalanda district — the same district as the current incident — fell ill after eating mid-day meals at a government school. The National Human Rights Commission took suo motu cognizance, issuing a formal notice to the Nalanda District Magistrate and demanding a detailed report within two weeks.

In February 2026, over 70 students at an upgraded middle school in Madhepura's Sadar block fell sick after their meal was allegedly contaminated — locals reported finding a lizard in the food. In June, 250 schoolchildren in Saharsa were hospitalised after suspected food poisoning from their mid-day meal.

The darkest chapter remains the 2013 tragedy in Gandamal village, Saran district, where 23 children between the ages of 5 and 12 died after eating a school lunch contaminated with the pesticide monocrotophos. The cooking oil had been stored near a pesticide container at the school headmistress's home. That incident triggered nationwide outrage and calls for reform of the programme's safety protocols.

Systemic Gaps in Food Safety

India's mid-day meal scheme, officially known as PM POSHAN (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman), is one of the world's largest school feeding programmes, serving approximately 120 million children across the country daily. It serves a dual purpose: improving nutrition among schoolchildren and incentivising attendance, particularly in states like Bihar where poverty rates remain high.

"The cook has been removed from duty. We are taking the matter seriously. Fortunately, all the kids are currently out of danger."

— District official, following a similar detergent-salt incident in West Bengal (2022)

But the programme has been plagued by recurring lapses. Investigations into past incidents have pointed to common failures: lack of proper storage facilities forcing schools to keep food supplies alongside cleaning agents and chemicals; absence of mandatory tasting by supervising teachers before meals are served; inadequate training for cooks; and weak enforcement of hygiene standards at the school level.

Why It Matters to the Diaspora

For members of the Indian diaspora — particularly those with roots in Bihar, one of the largest source states for emigration — incidents like these underscore persistent gaps in public services that affect their extended families back home. The mid-day meal scheme is widely regarded as one of India's most important welfare programmes, and its failures carry emotional weight for NRIs who grew up benefiting from similar government school programmes.

The recurring nature of these incidents raises questions about whether systemic reforms — centralised kitchens, third-party quality audits, and digital monitoring of food supply chains — have been implemented at scale or remain confined to policy documents. Bihar's state government will face renewed pressure to demonstrate accountability and prevent what has become a recurring crisis in its schools.
